bibl.title: Conversational Agents in Education – A Systematic Literature Review

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: critique
span.quote: Overall, we detected a deficiency of solidly validated studies of CAs.

span.label: pedagogical conversational agents in education
span.quote: There is a recent trend of increasing publications and implementations of CAs in education.

span.label: systematic-review
span.quote: To contribute to future research, we conducted an SLR based on Webster and Watson (2002), Page et al. (2021), and Schoormann et al. (2021).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Research projects design pedagogical CAs for short-run demonstration rather than sustained use, so the agents are not maintained past the prototype and fail soon after deployment.
span.quote: Since Janssen et al. (2021) proved that most CAs nevertheless fail within a short period, we reckon that this might particularly go back to the rare long-term orientation of the research projects outlined above.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Designers draw on only isolated fragments of the psychological/learning knowledge base, so the resulting agents realise only part of their potential.
span.quote: articles that are based upon psychological concepts and theories, however, usually only consider isolated aspects (e.g., CAs to promote improved multimedia learning), while a more diverse consideration of the knowledge base was hard to find. For this reason, we assume that existing CAs do not yet realise their full potential.

span.label: Selection and analysis rested on the authors' subjective decisions, mitigated but not removed by peer-reviewed screening and two coding waves.
span.note: what this limits: every inclusion and coding decision: INESCAPABLE LIMITATIONS REGARDING SUBJECTIVELY DRIVEN DECISIONS DURING THE SLR, reduced by peer review rather than removed
span.quote: In spite of inescapable limitations regarding subjectively driven decisions during the SLR, we purposefully undertook measures to reduce these through a peer-reviewed process in screening, two successive coding waves in an interdisciplinary research team, after querying seven scientific databases.

span.label: Relevant publications may have been missed during screening despite the breadth of databases and search terms.
span.note: what this limits: the completeness of the survey: IT IS STILL POSSIBLE THAT RELEVANT PUBLICATIONS MIGHT HAVE BEEN OVERLOOKED DURING THE SCREENING PROCESS
span.quote: Second, despite our extensive review of 252 publications, it is still possible that relevant publications might have been overlooked during the screening process, even though we included a variety of databases and search terms.

span.label: The review captures only a fast-moving field's current state; later searches may give different results.
span.note: what this limits: the shelf life of the findings: AS THE FIELD IS EVOLVING QUICKLY, WE CAN ONLY PROVIDE THE CURRENT STATE OF THE FIELD AND FUTURE SEARCHES ... MIGHT YIELD DIFFERENT RESULTS
span.quote: Ultimately, as the field is evolving quickly, we can only provide the current state of the field and future searches on related topics might yield different results.

span.label: The overview of the field excludes every publication not in English or German, so the reported state of the art is bounded by the reviewers' languages.
span.note: what this limits: this review as a holistic overview of conversational agents in education: publications in any language other than English or German were excluded by the stated criteria
span.quote: The following exclusion criteria were applied: missing educational context, no relation to CAs, another language than English or German

span.label: The review declares its own selection subjective, and states that this is normal for the method rather than particular to this team.
span.note: what this limits: the coverage of any systematic literature review including this one: the authors state the selection and analysis process rests on subjective decisions, as is common for SLRs
span.quote: First, as is common for SLRs, the selection and analysis process is based on subjective decisions of the authors

span.label: The claim about the field's maturity is an inference from how often software names recur, not a measurement of the systems.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that pedagogical conversational agents remain prototypes: it is an assumption drawn from software names being referenced only once and not developed in later publications
span.quote: although a large proportion of these software names are only referenced once, and have mostly not yet been further developed in subsequent publications. Thus, we assume that many pedagogical CAs are still in a prototypical stage

span.label: The review's own object is defined by publication facts as much as by content: papers in any language other than English or German are excluded, as is everything published before 2016. A reader takes the resulting picture as the state of the field, and the record already carries that reading as a sense.
span.quote: The following exclusion criteria were applied: missing educational context, no relation to CAs, another language than English or German, duplicates, language learning or health focus, as well as publications before 2016

span.label: exclusion criteria
span.quote: The following exclusion criteria were applied: missing educational context, no relation to CAs, another language than English or German

span.label: pedagogical CAs
span.quote: Thus, we assume that many pedagogical CAs are still in a prototypical stage

span.label: systematic literature
span.quote: a structured holistic overview of the scientific literature of CAs in the educational context is lacking.

span.label: prototype development
span.quote: Concerning the applied research methods, 95 papers use prototype development ( e.g., Sjöström and Dahlin, 2020; Al Muid et al., 2021). For the evaluation of the developed artefacts, researchers use mainly a quantitative approach (61 articles), and less frequently

span.label: state of the art in pedagogical conversational agents - AS VISIBLE THROUGH THIS REVIEW: what seven databases return, filtered to English and German, and screened by subjective decisions
span.quote: The exclusion was guided by pre-defined criteria, to ensure the fit with our RQ and the topicality of the contributions examined.

span.label: maturity of a pedagogical conversational agent - inferred from BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECURRENCE: a system named once and not developed further is taken as evidence of a prototype stage
span.quote: although a large proportion of these software names are only referenced once, and have mostly not yet been further developed in subsequent publications.

span.label: research method - in this field mostly PROTOTYPE DEVELOPMENT (95 of 252 papers), evaluated mainly quantitatively; so 'method' here names what was BUILT more often than what was tested
span.quote: Concerning the applied research methods, 95 papers use prototype development ( e.g., Sjöström and Dahlin, 2020; Al Muid et al., 2021). For the evaluation of the developed artefacts, researchers use mainly a quantitative approach (61 articles), and less frequently

span.label: builds-on → Webster and Watson (2002), Page et al. (2021), and Schoormann et al. (2021)
span.quote: To contribute to future research, we conducted an SLR based on Webster and Watson (2002), Page et al. (2021), and Schoormann et al. (2021).

span.label: extends → Gubareva and Lopes (2020) role taxonomy for pedagogical conversational agents
span.quote: Supplementary, we added the moderator function, because Gubareva and Lopes (2020) focused on academic student support and we covered a broader scope, also including the instructors’ perspective (e.g., Mikic-Fonte et al., 2019; Sakr et al., 2021).

span.label: replicates → Strohmann (2021) and Diederich et al. (2022)
span.quote: Similar to Strohmann (2021) and Diederich et al. (2022), we found that scenarios of the longterm orientation of CAs have so far been rarely considered, which is reflected in the lack of long-term studies (Diederich et al. 2022).

span.label: contradicts → cross-domain conversational-agent literature reviews (Diederich et al., 2022)
span.quote: However, contrary to what cross-domain literature reviews reveal, there is a difference in the quality of existing studies: While for CAs in general, a plethora of empirical studies with validated constructs exist (Diederich et al., 2022), those are underrepresented in the educational domain - many publications lack evaluations with a solid sample size.

span.label: exclusion criteria —operationalised-as→ pedagogical CAs
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE OBJECT OF THE REVIEW IS CONSTITUTED BY THIS LIST. Six criteria decide what counts as the field: educational context, relation to CAs, ENGLISH OR GERMAN ONLY, no duplicates, NOT language learning, NOT health, and NOTHING BEFORE 2016. Two of those - the language filter and the 2016 cut - are about where and when a paper was published rather than what it says. The record already carries a sense reading the state of the art as visible THROUGH these criteria.
span.quote: The following exclusion criteria were applied: missing educational context, no relation to CAs, another language than English or German, duplicates, language learning or health focus, as well as publications before 2016

span.label: exclusion criteria —part-of→ systematic literature
span.note: differs in: THE SIZE OF THE FUNNEL: 3,329 records found, 252 finally coded. The field as reported is 7.6% of the field as retrieved, and the other 92% is removed by criteria rather than by reading · strength of the relation: 0.8
span.quote: The initially found 3329 records were systematically reduced to 252 fully coded articles

span.label: Only five of the 252 coded articles reported long-term studies of conversational agents in education.
span.quote: Only five studies out of 252 articles reported on long-term studies

span.label: Pedagogical CAs act most often as tutors (31%), then as motivators and organizers (21% each), mentors (18%) and moderators (9%).
span.quote: The distribution of the roles is as follows: 31% tutor, 21% motivator, 21% organizer, 18% mentor, 9% moderator.

span.label: Academic students are the target group in 78% of the studies, with school students, teachers, professionals and others each accounting for only about 5-6%.
span.quote: The target groups addressed by the CAs in the analysed sample are: 78% academic students (e.g., Mikic-Fonte et al., 2019; Sakr et al., 2021), 6% high school students or equivalent

span.label: The word "chatbot" appears in 167 of the 252 articles (85%) while "virtual companion(ship)" appears in only 2 articles, showing the companion framing is nearly absent from the education literature.
span.quote: While the term "chatbot" was used in 167 publications and thus a majority of the 252 articles (85%) with a total of 5661 entries, the term "virtual companion(ship)" appeared in only 2 articles (< 1%) with 28 overall mentions

span.label: 136 of the reviewed publications cite psychological or learning theory, and 80% of the cited theories come from educational research rather than from psychology or HCI.
span.quote: In 136 of the reviewed publications, we identified theoretical reflections referencing psychological or learning pedagogical theories on the topic of CAs in the educational setting. The majority of mentioned theories (80%) stem from educational research.

span.label: Google Dialogflow (37%) and IBM Watson Assistant (30%) are the two building platforms most often used to implement pedagogical CAs.
span.quote: we analysed which platforms were mentioned most frequently: Google Dialogflow (37%) (e.g., Gonda and Chu, 2019; El Hefny et al., 2021) and IBM Watson Assistant (30%) (e.g., Ralston et al., 2019; Oliveira et al., 2019).

span.label: Most of the reviewed studies evaluate their agents on small samples, so their results may not be representative.
span.quote: Furthermore, the majority of the studies have a small sample size, so the representativeness of the results must be further examined.

span.label: Exactly one of the 252 papers offers prescriptive design knowledge in the form of a nascent design theory, and it is confined to argumentation skills.
span.quote: Only one paper presents a (nascent) design theory as prescriptive design knowledge (Gregor, 2002; Gregor and Hevner, 2013), focusing on the advancement of argumentation skills as a specific application context

span.label: Only 5% of the articles address professional development outside academia, leaving lifelong and vocational learning largely unstudied.
span.quote: Only 5% of the articles cover professional development in a non-academic context

span.label: A large share of the reviewed authors design their conversational agent without grounding it in any scientific theory.
span.quote: We found that a large number of authors do not base the design of their CA on scientific theories.

span.label: conversational agent (CA)
span.quote: CA is an umbrella term for software that uses natural language to interact with its user, either text-based (as chatbots) or speechbased (as virtual assistants) (McTear et al., 2016; Gnewuch et al., 2017).

span.label: pedagogical conversational agent
span.quote: developing area is the use of "pedagogical CAs" which are e-learning systems, that “interact with learners using natural language dialogs” (Hobert and von Wolff, 2019, p. 301).

span.label: virtual companion
span.quote: which are referred to as "virtual companions" that build friendships with their users since they enable the establishment of a collaborative bond

span.label: social cues
span.quote: an essential way to implement anthropomorphism in a CA, is the use of "social cues", in terms of "signals depicted by humans when interacting with each other" (El Hefny et al., 2021, p. 675)

span.label: computers as social actors (CASA)
span.quote: This finding is supported by the theory of Nass et al. (1994) and Moon (2000), which states that people tend to treat “computers as social actors” (CASA) if they exhibit human-like characteristics.

span.label: 252 — number of articles fully coded in the review after screening
span.quote: Based on the pre-defined exclusion criteria, we finally reduced the data set to 252 articles that were fully analyzed by five coding scientists using the software MAXQDA as suggested by Bandara et al. (2015).

span.label: 3891 — total records returned by the database search before screening
span.quote: The search query resulted in a total of 3891 hits.

span.label: 95 — papers whose research method is prototype development
span.quote: Concerning the applied research methods, 95 papers use prototype development

span.label: 82 — studies that include an experimental setting
span.quote: 82 studies include an experimental setting to test their assumptions

span.label: 18 — papers that explicitly follow a user-centred design approach
span.quote: we found 18 papers explicitly mentioning a user-centred design approach

span.label: five — studies out of 252 that were long-term studies
span.quote: Only five studies out of 252 articles reported on long-term studies

span.label: 78% — share of studies whose target group is academic students
span.quote: The target groups addressed by the CAs in the analysed sample are: 78% academic students (e.g., Mikic-Fonte et al., 2019; Sakr et al., 2021), 6% high school students or equivalent

span.label: 80% — share of the cited theories that originate in educational research
span.quote: In 136 of the reviewed publications, we identified theoretical reflections referencing psychological or learning pedagogical theories on the topic of CAs in the educational setting. The majority of mentioned theories (80%) stem from educational research.

span.label: 37% — share of implementations using Google Dialogflow as building platform
span.quote: we analysed which platforms were mentioned most frequently: Google Dialogflow (37%) (e.g., Gonda and Chu, 2019; El Hefny et al., 2021) and IBM Watson Assistant (30%) (e.g., Ralston et al., 2019; Oliveira et al., 2019).

span.label: 31% — share of pedagogical CAs occupying the tutor role
span.quote: The distribution of the roles is as follows: 31% tutor, 21% motivator, 21% organizer, 18% mentor, 9% moderator.
